developer-foundations-mock3-5.rationale: A well-formed, complete, but wrong answer points to what the model was told, so inspect the prompt and the context built for that input (B). Transport (A) and rate limits (C) cause failures of delivery, and end_turn shows the reply was not truncated (D).
developer-foundations-mock3-5.evidence: Check stop_reason first; if the response completed normally, inspect the prompt and inputs for that request.

developer-foundations-mock3-6.question: A team puts its FAQ lookup on the top-tier model because it has the largest context window, though no prompt in the product exceeds 6K tokens. What is the practical consequence?

options.A: Better accuracy on short prompts, because spare capacity goes to deeper reasoning
options.B: Fewer 429 errors, because requests land in a larger rate-limit bucket
options.C: More reliable structured output, because longer windows enforce schemas better
options.D: Higher cost and latency for a capability the task never uses

developer-foundations-mock3-6.rationale: Unused capacity is still paid for, in higher price and slower responses (D). A bigger window does not by itself improve short-prompt accuracy (A), enlarge rate limits (B), or make schemas more reliable (C).
developer-foundations-mock3-6.evidence: Choose the model that meets your quality bar at the lowest cost and latency.

developer-foundations-mock3-7.question: Spend on a Sonnet-based triage feature doubled after launch, and a manager asks to move it to Haiku. How should the team decide?

options.A: Run the feature's eval set on Haiku and move only if it meets the stated quality bar
options.B: Move as soon as monthly spend passes the budget line that was set at launch
options.C: Move whenever volume passes 1M calls a month, since volume favors small models
options.D: Move once users start complaining about response time in support tickets

developer-foundations-mock3-7.rationale: The move is an evidence-led decision against a defined quality bar (A). Budget overruns (B), high volume (C), and latency complaints (D) are reasons to look at a smaller tier, but none shows that quality holds.
developer-foundations-mock3-7.evidence: Evaluate smaller models on your own task; move down a tier only when it meets your quality threshold.

developer-foundations-mock3-8.question: A research agent runs 200 steps with context compaction enabled. At step 20 it decided to exclude all pre-2020 sources, and by step 150 it is citing 2017 papers. What is the correct mechanism?

options.A: Rely on the long context window to keep the decision visible
options.B: Add 'remember all earlier decisions' to the system prompt
options.C: Write the decision to explicit state or a notes store that is re-injected each turn
options.D: Restart the agent every 50 steps, re-supplying the original task description each time

developer-foundations-mock3-8.rationale: Durable decisions must live in explicit state outside the compactable history, because context is finite and compaction is lossy (C). The window (A) is exactly what compaction rewrites, a reminder (B) cannot restore a lost fact, and restarting (D) throws the decision away.
developer-foundations-mock3-8.evidence: Agents persist notes outside the context window and pull them back in later; compaction summaries can lose detail.

developer-foundations-mock3-9.question: An invoice pipeline always runs extract, validate, then post, and a teammate wants to call it an agent. What distinguishes a workflow from an agent in practice?

options.A: Workflows run fewer steps, while agents are defined as anything running more than ten
options.B: Agents are the only pattern that can call tools; workflows only call the model
options.C: Workflows keep state in a database, while agents hold state only in the context window
options.D: Code fixes a workflow's control flow, while an agent's model chooses the next step

developer-foundations-mock3-9.rationale: The distinction is who decides the next step: predefined code paths for workflows, model-directed process for agents (D). Step count (A), tool access (B), and where state is stored (C) are incidental, since workflows call tools and agents may use databases.
developer-foundations-mock3-9.evidence: Workflows orchestrate LLMs and tools through predefined code paths; agents dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage.

developer-foundations-mock3-10.question: A classification prompt says 'answer with a single lowercase label', but its three examples show 'Label: Billing' in title case plus a sentence of explanation. Outputs vary from run to run. What is the likely outcome of this contradiction?

options.A: The explicit instruction wins on every run, since it is stated directly
options.B: The examples win on every run, because concrete examples outweigh instructions
options.C: Output flips between the instruction's format and the examples' format
options.D: The API rejects the request with a validation error about conflicting guidance

developer-foundations-mock3-10.rationale: Contradictory signals produce inconsistent behavior with no defined precedence, so some runs follow the instruction and others the examples (C). Neither the instruction (A) nor the examples (B) reliably wins, and the API does not validate prompt consistency (D).
developer-foundations-mock3-10.evidence: Make sure examples match the behavior you want; Claude pays close attention to examples, so conflicts cause inconsistency.

developer-foundations-mock3-11.question: A 150-page contract is pasted into the prompt, with the one rule that matters (never disclose party names) placed in the middle of the document. Outputs sometimes disclose names. What is the effect of that placement?

options.A: None, since where an instruction sits in a prompt does not affect how well it is followed
options.B: It is more likely to be overlooked than if placed at the start or end of the prompt
options.C: It is followed more closely, because the surrounding text gives the rule context
options.D: The middle is silently truncated, which drops the rule before generation begins

developer-foundations-mock3-11.rationale: In long inputs, material buried in the middle is attended to less reliably than material at the edges, so critical rules belong in the system prompt or after the document (B). Position does matter (A) and does not help here (C), and over-long prompts error rather than silently truncate (D).
developer-foundations-mock3-11.evidence: Put long documents at the top and the instructions or question at the end; critical instructions buried mid-context are easier to miss.

developer-foundations-mock3-12.question: A search_files tool returns each match with its full 30 KB body, but the agent normally just passes a match to a later read_file call. When should a tool return an identifier instead of the full object?

options.A: When the object is large and the model only needs it to reference in a later call
options.B: Only on write operations, because reads must return the complete object to be usable
options.C: Always, since a smaller tool result is cheaper whatever the task needs
options.D: Never, because the model cannot call a second tool using an ID it was given

developer-foundations-mock3-12.rationale: Returning a handle keeps context free when the payload is only needed to refer to the object later (A). Restricting the rule to writes (B), applying it always (C), or banning it (D) ignores what the task actually requires from the result.
developer-foundations-mock3-12.evidence: Prefer meaningful, high-signal identifiers and return only what the agent needs; let it fetch details in a follow-up call.

developer-foundations-mock3-13.question: After you connect a third-party MCP server exposing 18 tools, your agent's task success falls from 91% to 74%. Traces show no errors or timeouts, but the agent often calls a tool that does not fit the step it is on. What should you check first?

options.A: Whether the new tools overlap and have distinguishable descriptions
options.B: The server's uptime and restart history over the last 30 days of operation
options.C: Whether the pinned model ID now silently resolves to a different model version
options.D: Whether the server's tool results are large enough to push the instructions out of context

developer-foundations-mock3-13.rationale: Calls that succeed but pick the wrong tool point at tool selection: a larger, overlapping tool surface with unclear descriptions is the usual cause (A). Downtime (B) would show up as errors, a pinned model ID (C) does not change underneath you, and oversized results (D) would degrade later steps rather than the choice of tool itself.
developer-foundations-mock3-13.evidence: Too many overlapping tools with unclear descriptions confuse agents; consolidate and describe each distinctly.

developer-foundations-mock3-14.question: A feature inserts Claude's reply into a web page through innerHTML. A user pastes text asking Claude to include a script tag in its answer. What must the application do?

options.A: Nothing extra, since models are trained not to emit executable markup
options.B: Treat the reply as untrusted and sanitize it before rendering
options.C: Add a system prompt rule forbidding HTML and rely on the model to comply
options.D: Ask a second Claude call whether the reply is safe and render it if it says yes

developer-foundations-mock3-14.rationale: Anything rendered into a page is escaped or sanitized regardless of source, because model output can be shaped by user input (B). Assuming safety (A), a prompt rule (C), and an LLM safety check (D) are not deterministic controls.
developer-foundations-mock3-14.evidence: Treat model output as untrusted input to downstream systems; sanitize it before rendering or executing.

developer-foundations-mock3-15.question: A prompt tweak raised invoice-total accuracy from 88% to 94% on the target eval, and two weeks later support found that date extraction had slipped. What does a regression suite protect against that the one-off eval did not?

options.A: Slower responses caused by a longer prompt and extra reasoning tokens
options.B: Rate limit errors when the evaluation is run at higher volume than before
options.C: A change that improves the targeted behavior while silently breaking another behavior
options.D: Cost increases from higher token usage after the change shipped to production

developer-foundations-mock3-15.rationale: Regressions are silent by definition and are caught by continuously re-testing the behaviors that must not break (C). Latency (A), rate limits (B), and cost (D) are operational signals rather than correctness checks.
developer-foundations-mock3-15.evidence: Run your eval set on every change so improvements in one area do not mask regressions in another.
